effects.log: {npc} stops the merchant, reads the ledgers in the cart, and lets the merchant go with an apology and an escort. You are almost disappointed. You had hoped for a reason to dislike {him}.

choices.text: Drive {him} off the ridge. Robbery is robbery

effects.log: A rockfall closes the caves. {npc} moves {his} band to the next county, and the doorsteps of the village stop finding rice, and the poorest houses blame the ridge.

events.text: A royal commander with five hundred men has sealed the valley to take {npc}. They are going house to house in the village, asking who took the rice, and the rice is still in the jars. By evening someone will talk. {npc} has come out of the caves to the ridge shrine and is sitting there with {his} sword across {his} knees.

choices.text: "Go over the pass tonight. I will close it behind you"

effects.log: A landslide closes the pass an hour after {npc} and the forty cross it. The commander searches the valley for a month, finds rice in every jar and nobody who knows where it came from, and leaves.

choices.text: "Give yourself up. Save the village"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time, then nods, and walks down to the commander with the sword held out hilt first. The village is left alone. You go into the commander's dreams for a year after, until the sentence is changed to exile.

choices.text: Speak to the commander from the sky

effects.log: The commander is a brave person and stands in the rain listening to a dragon explain the tax-grain accounts of the province. Then the commander sends a report to the court that names the landlords instead of the outlaw.

events.text: {npc} is old, grey, limping, and has come back over the pass alone. The band is long gone; the landlords are mostly dead; one of them, {he} admits, was not as bad as {he} thought. {He} wants to be buried on your ridge, near the caves, with no stone.

choices.text: "Stay, and keep the caves"

effects.npcPass: old age, in the caves, keeping them
effects.log: {npc} lives in the caves ten more years, growing beans, telling stories to the boys of the village that grow better every telling. {He} is buried there with no stone, as asked. Every boy in the village knows the place.

choices.text: "Go down to the village. They remember the rice"

effects.npcPass: old age, in a house in the village
effects.log: They remember. A house is found, and a bowl, and a seat at the threshing floor at every festival. {npc} dies there, warm, much embarrassed by the attention.

events.text: Two immortals have sat down on a flat stone on your back to play baduk: white beards, cloud robes, one with a gourd, one with a fan, clicking stones onto the board very slowly. A young woodcutter came up the path with an axe, stopped to watch, and has been watching ever since. To him it has been an hour. It has been three days. The handle of the axe he is leaning on has begun, very slowly, to turn to dust.

choices.text: Shrug, gently, so the woodcutter stumbles and looks up

effects.log: He staggers, looks at his axe, looks at the sky, and runs down the mountain, three days late for supper and very confused. The immortals glare at you. "It was a good game," says the one with the fan. "He was learning something."

choices.text: Lie still. A good game should not be interrupted

effects.log: You lie still and watch the game too. It is very beautiful, the black and the white, the long slow fight for a corner. When at last it ends you look round, and the woodcutter is still there, and the axe handle is gone.

choices.text: Ask to play the winner

ok.log: The game you play takes a year and you lose by half a stone, and the immortal with the gourd says it is the best game a dragon has ever played, which is to say, the only one. The woodcutter, distracted by the novelty, goes home only a month late.

fail.log: You lose in forty moves. The immortals are delighted and set up another game at once. The woodcutter, enthralled, does not move.

events.text: The woodcutter goes home down the mountain with an axe head and no handle, to a village he does not recognise. Strangers in his house. A great-great-grandchild, very old, is told the story of a young ancestor who went up the dragon ridge to cut wood and never came back, and here he is, at the gate, younger than everyone.

choices.text: Go down and explain, as well as anyone can

effects.log: You tell them in a dream, all of them at once. In the morning the family takes him in, the youngest great-great-great-grandfather in the province. He lives a long time and is very good with children, being, in many ways, one.

choices.text: Let him find his own way in his own century

effects.log: He becomes a story: the woodcutter who watched the immortals play. He tells it himself, in the market, for coppers, for years, and never gets it quite right, because he missed the end of the game.

events.text: The immortal with the gourd comes back alone, sets the board on the flat stone on your back, and taps it. "A game," it says. "No woodcutters this time. Just you. You have learned something since, I think. Show me."

choices.text: Play to win

ok.log: You win by a stone and a half after a hundred years of play. The immortal looks at the board for a long time, then sweeps the stones into the bowls. "Again," it says. You are not sure whether it is pleased.

fail.log: You lose, as you lose every time. The immortal hums. "You still play like a dragon," it says. "All attack, no corners." It is the most useful thing anyone has said to you in a thousand years.

choices.text: Play to learn, and give away the corners

effects.log: You lose beautifully. The immortal laughs aloud for the first time in your acquaintance. "There," it says. "Now you play like the east. Everything given, and still the board is yours." Somewhere a season turns.

events.text: A light falls out of heaven at the sea mouth: a pearl the size of a man's head, burning white, the wish-pearl that dragons are painted holding. And from the southern islands, faster than you, comes a black dragon, lean as a whip, racing for it. "It is mine!" it shouts across the storm. It is younger than you. It might be right.

choices.text: Race for it

ok.log: You take it out of the air a length ahead of the black dragon. It burns in your claw, warm, alive, full of every wish anyone ever made. The black dragon screams and goes back south. You have the pearl. Now you have to decide what a pearl is for.

fail.log: The black dragon is faster and wants it more. It takes the pearl a breath ahead of you and lashes you across the face with its tail for good measure. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the black dragon have it

effects.log: You slow, on purpose, and the black dragon takes it and stops in the air, astonished, looking back at you. It does not thank you. But it does not forget.

choices.text: Stop and ask whose it is

effects.log: While you are asking, the black dragon takes it. But you see, below, in the sea mouth, an old grey serpent with its head out of the water, watching the pearl go, with the face of something that has waited a very long time.

events.text: You have the pearl, and everyone knows it. Kings send envoys. Sects send thieves. Your valley asks for rain, health, sons, a new bridge, and you could give every wish. At the sea mouth an old grey serpent, an imugi that has waited a thousand years, has come up out of the deep and lies on the rocks without asking for anything. A pearl from heaven, the old stories say, is how a serpent becomes a dragon. This one fell where it lay.

choices.text: Give the pearl to the serpent

effects.log: You lay it in front of the old grey head. It looks at you for a long time. Then it takes the pearl in its mouth, and the sea mouth goes white, and a new dragon rises out of the storm, grey and enormous, weeping. It bows to you once, and goes up.

choices.text: Keep it, and grant the valley's wishes, carefully

effects.log: One wish a year, small ones: a bridge, a well, a fever lifted. The valley becomes the luckiest in the land. The pearl grows a little dimmer each time, and you grow a little prouder, and the serpent at the sea mouth goes back down into the deep.

choices.text: Throw it back into the sky

effects.log: It goes up like a star in reverse and does not come down. Wherever it went, it went without you holding it. You feel very light afterwards, and a little foolish, and right.

events.text: The black dragon of the southern islands comes north to find you, a hundred years older and no longer lean. It lands on your ridge and folds itself up awkwardly. "About the pearl," it says. "I have been thinking about it for a century. I want to know what you would have done with it."

choices.text: Tell it honestly

effects.log: You tell it the truth, which is that you do not know. The black dragon laughs, a sound like surf on rocks. "Neither did I," it says. "I kept it in a cave for a hundred years and was afraid to wish." It stays a season. You are friends, more or less, after that.

choices.text: Challenge it to a race, for no pearl at all

ok.log: Round the eastern sea and back, for nothing. You win by a whisker. It wins the next one. You race every century after, and the fishermen of three coasts time their seasons by it.

fail.log: It wins easily, still faster. It is delighted. You are, unexpectedly, delighted too.

events.text: A grandmaster has climbed the highest peak in the land, above the clouds, to stand where the Flying Dragon passes: the strongest sword of the age, white-haired, unbeaten for forty years and bored to death of it. "Nobody on the ground is worth drawing for," {npc} calls into the wind. "Come down, dragon. One exchange. I want to know if I am anything."
events.arc: The Grandmaster Who Climbed the Clouds

choices.text: Give {him} the exchange

mem.note: gave me the one exchange I wanted

ok.log: One cut, one strike of a five-clawed foot, a sound like a mountain cracking. When the cloud settles {npc} is on {his} back in the snow, laughing, sword broken, and there is a fine line cut in the scales of your foreleg. "Something," {he} says. "I am something."

fail.log: The best sword of the age is very, very good.
fail.deathCause: the sword of a grandmaster above the clouds

choices.text: "You are something. Go home and teach it"

effects.log: {npc} stands in the wind a long time, sword half drawn. Then {he} sheathes it. "Teaching," {he} says, as if tasting a new word. {He} goes down the mountain. Twenty years later there are three swordsmen in the land almost as good as {him}.

choices.text: Fly past without stopping

effects.log: You go by like weather. {npc} watches you go, and sits down in the snow, and laughs until {he} cries. "Not even worth stopping for," {he} says. "Good. Good. I needed that."

events.text: A young swordsman climbs the same peak above the clouds with a broken sword wrapped in silk: {npc}'s, the grandmaster's, dead now, very old, in bed, to everyone's surprise. The young one is the last student. "My teacher said to bring it back to you," the student says. "And to say: thank you for the answer."
events.arc: The Grandmaster Who Climbed the Clouds

choices.text: Take the broken sword and keep it in the clouds

effects.npcPass: old age, in bed, to everyone's surprise
effects.log: It lies in the heart of a cloud on the eastern sky for a thousand years. Sometimes, in a storm, a swordsman on the ground sees the gleam and thinks it is lightning.

choices.text: Give the student the exchange the teacher had

ok.npcPass: old age, in bed, to everyone's surprise
ok.log: A gentle one: you let the student touch your foreleg once with the flat of the blade, on the old scar. The student goes down the mountain different. In a few years it is the best sword of a new age.

fail.npcPass: old age, in bed, to everyone's surprise
fail.log: The student cuts too hard, out of grief, and you have to knock the blade away. Nobody is hurt. The student weeps on the summit, and you stay until it is over.

events.text: The second moon, and on the windy island in the southern sea the Wind Grandmother comes in on her own gale, as she does every year: white hair streaming, a basket on her hip, sowing seeds of shells and sea grass over the sea floor for the divers to harvest. The island's divers make her a rite on the black rocks. She looks up at you in the sky with a sharp old eye. "Land spring," she says. "Everybody sings about land spring. Who sings for the sea?"

choices.text: "You do. Teach me the sea spring"

effects.log: She takes you down under the waves for the whole of her two weeks: the kelp waking, the abalone, the divers going down on one breath with their nets. When she leaves on her straw boat she says you are a slow learner and a good one.

choices.text: Sing for the sea yourself, with the island's rite

ok.log: The shaman on the rocks hears something under the drums: a long low voice singing for the sea. The divers have the best season in living memory. The Wind Grandmother sniffs and says it was adequate.

fail.log: Your song comes out as a spring thunderstorm, which is the wrong season for the sea. The Wind Grandmother laughs so hard her gale blows the offerings off the rocks.

choices.text: "The east wind is mine. Your gale is late"

effects.log: She sets down her basket and blows. You spend three days in a typhoon you did not order, learning that an old woman with a gale is not to be argued with in her own month.

events.text: The farewell rite on the island: the oldest men push a little straw boat loaded with rice cakes out into the waves to carry the Wind Grandmother home, and the shaman scatters millet seed on a mat to read the year from where it falls. The Wind Grandmother sits in the straw boat, which is far too small for her, and beckons you down. "Read the seeds with me," she says. "It is my last year. Someone has to know how."

choices.text: Learn to read the seeds

effects.log: The millet on the mat is a map: here the shoals, here the storm, here a diver who must not go out on the ninth day. Next year the shaman reads it, and you read it with her, and the diver stays home.

choices.text: "Not your last. Come back in spring, with me"

effects.log: "Spring is your business," she says, but she comes back, in the second moon, a little smaller, on a softer wind. The island says the grandmother has grown gentle. She says she has grown lazy, and has a dragon to help.

events.text: The first day of spring by the old calendar, and the people of every village in the land are writing the same four characters and pasting them on their gates: GREAT LUCK AT THE START OF SPRING. Ten thousand gates, a hundred thousand, all addressed to you, as if spring could be invited by letter. In one village one gate is bare. Behind it a family in mourning white has not felt like writing anything this year.

choices.text: Go to the bare gate first

effects.log: You come in through the bare gate as a warm wind, and the plum by the kitchen opens one bud, and a child in white sees it and runs to tell the others. Nobody writes anything. Nobody needs to.

choices.text: Come to every gate at once, as you always do

effects.log: Spring comes everywhere on the same morning, to every gate, written or not. It is what you are. The bare gate gets it too. You hope that is enough.

choices.text: Write the four characters yourself, in frost, on the bare gate

ok.log: In the morning there they are on the bare gate, in frost-white, in a hand nobody in the village has. They melt by noon. The family talks about them for the rest of their lives, and writes them again the next year themselves.

fail.log: The frost characters come out slightly wrong, the way a child writes them. The family laughs for the first time since the funeral. Perhaps that was the point.

events.text: The third day of the third moon: the swallows come back from the far south, the girls fry azalea petals on rice cakes, and everyone walks out on the new green. One swallow is late, and lands on your wind with a mended leg, bound with thread and a twig. A poor farmer did it, it tells you, last autumn, a man too poor to feed his own children, who still had thread for a bird. "I want to give him something," it says. "I am a swallow. I have nothing. You are spring."

choices.text: Give it a gourd seed full of spring

effects.log: The swallow drops it in the poor man's yard. A gourd vine comes up over the roof in a week, and in autumn the gourds are as big as rice jars. When he saws them open, they are full of rice. Only rice. He weeps anyway; it is what he needed.

choices.text: Give it a good season for him, nothing magic

effects.log: His field has the best year in the village and nobody can explain it. He thanks heaven. The swallow nests under his eaves every year after, and he never knows it is a messenger.

choices.text: "You are a swallow. Your thanks is to come back"

effects.log: The swallow thinks about this and comes back, every spring, to his eaves, for the rest of its life, and its children after it. The farmer considers this the luckiest thing that ever happened to him. He is right.

events.text: The poor farmer's rich brother has heard about the gourds. He has caught a swallow in his own yard, broken its leg on purpose, bound it with silk thread, and set it free with a great show of pity. The swallow comes to you limping. It does not want to give him anything. It is very frightened of him.

choices.text: Give the rich brother a gourd seed too

effects.log: His gourds grow as big as houses. When he saws them open, out come goblins with clubs, a flood of muddy water, and a moneylender with a ledger. He loses everything and goes to live with his poor brother, who takes him in. The story is told for a thousand years.

choices.text: Mend the swallow's leg yourself, and send it far away

effects.log: It flies south a month early, whole, and never comes back to his yard. His eaves stay empty for the rest of his life. He never knows why, which is the worst punishment you can think of for a man who must know everything.

events.text: The Seven Stars of the north come across the sky to the east one night, in a line, seven old spirits in white: the Dipper, who keep the length of human lives. Every night in ten thousand villages, mothers set out a bowl of clean water to them for their children's years. Tonight one mother's child is dying, and the seven have come to ask a strange favour: "Lend us your seven stars for one night. Fourteen is a stronger number than seven."
events.arc: The Seven Stars of the North

choices.text: Lend them, and let the east go dark for a night

effects.log: For one night the Eastern Palace is dark, and astronomers across the land write frightened reports, and a child with a fever opens its eyes and asks for water. In the morning your stars come back, a little brighter for the use.

choices.text: "Lives are yours to count, not mine"

effects.log: The seven bow and go back north. The child lives, or does not; you do not ask. You tell yourself it was not your mansion. It was not. You think about it for a long time anyway.

choices.text: Go yourself, as spring, to the child's room

effects.log: You come in through a crack in the paper door as a warm green breath, and the fever breaks like ice in a thaw. The seven stars watch from the window, and the eldest nods. "That works too," it says.

events.text: The child the Seven Stars saved is very old now, a grandmother of forty grandchildren, and every night she sets out two bowls of clean water on her terrace: one facing north, one facing east. Tonight she is dying, gently, and the seven old spirits have come for her, and they look at you, and at the second bowl.
events.arc: The Seven Stars of the North

choices.text: Drink from the east bowl, and let her go with the seven

effects.log: You drink the water and she sees you do it, and smiles, and goes north with the seven old men, holding the youngest one's sleeve. Forty grandchildren set out two bowls every night after.

choices.text: Blossom the plum by her terrace one last time

effects.log: In the middle of autumn the old plum by her terrace opens all at once. She looks at it, and laughs, and goes. The plum flowers every autumn after, out of season, and the family never explains it to anyone.

events.text: You are spring, and spring does not stop at the mountains. Far to the north, past the last rice field, past the last tiled roof, there is a grassland as wide as a sky, where herders live in felt tents and count the year by the foals. Here nobody calls you by any name at all. A mare is foaling in the last snow at dawn, and the herder kneeling beside her is praying to a sky that is, this morning, you.

choices.text: Come early here, a week before the east

effects.log: The snow goes off the grass a week early and the foal stands up on green. The herder sings a song in a language you have never heard. It is about you. It does not need your name.

choices.text: Come as the herders know you: a hard wind and then grass

effects.log: You learn the grassland spring: not blossom and rain, but a wind that hurts and then, all at once, grass to the horizon. It is a different spring. It is still you. You did not know you could be this.

events.text: Spring under the sea comes late and green: the kelp waking, the fish turning north, light coming down through the water a little longer every day. The Dragon King of the eastern sea receives you in his palace of coral with great formality, as one king receives another, and then, when the courtiers have gone, leans over and says: "You were an egg in a village well. I remember. I sent the rain that night."

choices.text: Thank him for the rain

effects.log: He waves it away, pleased. "Everybody forgets the rain," he says. "They remember the well." You stay a season in the coral palace, and learn how the sea does spring, slowly, from the bottom up.

choices.text: Ask him who laid the egg

effects.log: He looks at you a long time. "Nobody laid it," he says at last. "Spring wanted to be somebody for a while, and the well was there." You think about that for a hundred years, and it never stops being strange.

events.text: The ground shakes, and it is not you. A grandmother taller than the mountains is walking across the land with an apron full of boulders, as she did when the world was new and she set the hills where they are. She stops at your valley, squats down with a grunt, and looks at your old ridge. "Crooked," she says. "I always meant to fix that. Hold still."

choices.text: Hold still. She made the mountains

effects.log: She nudges your old ridge a hand to the left with her thumb. Every house in the village rattles. Afterwards the river runs a little straighter and the morning sun comes into the valley a quarter of an hour earlier, and nobody has ever been able to explain that either.

choices.text: "It is crooked because I lay there, Grandmother"

effects.log: She peers at you, close, with an eye the size of a pond. "Ah," she says. "So it is. Then it is the right kind of crooked." She pats the ridge, and gets up, and goes north, and an earthquake follows her like a dog.

choices.text: Ask her what she meant the world to be

effects.log: "Lived in," she says. "That is all. Mountains for the back, water for the front, something kind on the left and the right." She looks at you and the old White Tiger's ridge. "Good. That part worked."

events.text: The giant grandmother comes back older and much smaller, the size of a hill now, tired, her apron empty. She sits down on your old ridge with her back against the sky. "The world is made," she says. "Nobody needs a grandmother with boulders any more. They need spring. Tell me, is it tiring, being needed every year?"

choices.text: "Yes. It is the best thing I know"

effects.log: She laughs, and the hills echo it. "Good answer," she says. She sleeps on your ridge for a season, and when she goes, there is a new hill at the valley mouth, the shape of an old woman sleeping, and the children slide down it in winter.

choices.text: Lend her a spring of her own, on one hill

effects.log: You make one hill bloom for her alone, out of season, all azalea. She sits in it and cries a little, which is an earthquake in the next province. Afterwards she says it was the best present anyone ever gave her, including the mountains, which she gave to herself.

events.text: Cold Food Day, a hundred and five days after the solstice: no fires, cold mugwort cakes, families on every hill in the land weeding their graves. You are spring, so you are on every hill at once, and you find you know where they all are: the farmers, the potters and the singers, the hunters, the first hand that ever drew water. Thousands of years of people. Every one of them, today, under new grass.

choices.text: Visit every one, in order, all day

effects.log: It takes the whole day, being everywhere. Over each one you bring up one small green thing: a violet, a shoot of bracken, a single azalea. By dusk the hills are full of names nobody living remembers but you.

choices.text: Visit one: the grave of the first water

effects.log: An old grave by an old well, long ago flattened by ploughs, that nobody weeds because nobody knows. You know. You lie there all day as a warm wind, and in the evening the well water tastes, for one hour, like the first water of a year long gone.

choices.text: Let the living weed. Spring is for them

effects.log: You give the day to the living: the children sliding on the grave hills, the grandmothers unpacking cold cakes. The dead, you feel, would approve. Most of them were very practical people.

events.text: One year, for the first time in all your thousand years as spring, you do not want to come. Nothing is wrong. You are only tired, in a way no Dive cures: tired of beginning, every year, the same beginning. The ice stays on the paddies. The plum stays shut. In ten thousand villages people look at the sky and then at each other.

choices.text: Come anyway. That is what being spring means

effects.log: You come a week late, heavily, like an old farmer getting up before dawn. Nobody notices the difference except a few very old women, who say the spring is tired this year, and leave out extra rice.

choices.text: Rest one more week, and let them wait

effects.log: A week of hard frost in the third month. Some seedlings die. In a village you know, a child goes out into a frozen field with a stick and a handful of seeds and plants them anyway, alone, on principle.

choices.text: Ask the Black Tortoise to hold winter a little longer, for you

effects.log: The tortoise and the snake of the north look at you with something like tenderness. "Everybody gets tired," says the tortoise. "Even spring," says the snake. They hold winter, a week, carefully, so that nothing dies.

events.text: The child who planted seeds in the frozen field is grown, a farmer, and this spring stands at the edge of that same field at dawn as you come over the hills, on time, and says to the empty air: "I knew you would. I planted first anyway. I always do now. Just in case you are tired."

choices.text: Bring that field up first, every year, for the rest of that life

effects.log: Every spring for years, that field is the first green in the land. The farmer never says a word about it to anyone, and plants first, every year, just in case.

choices.text: Rest in the field for a day, as a warm wind, and let a human begin the spring

effects.log: For one day spring is something that is done to you, by a farmer with a stick, and you find it is the most restful day you have had in a thousand years.

events.text: Three messengers of the underworld in black robes and tall black hats stand at the gate of a cottage in the village with a summons in red. The old woman inside is ready to go, and tells them so, and asks for only one thing: to see the plum in the yard flower once more. It is late winter. The plum is ten days from flowering. The messengers have a schedule.

choices.text: Bring spring ten days early, to one tree

effects.log: The plum opens in the night, alone in a frozen village. She sits at the door in the morning and looks at it until noon, and then she gets up and goes out to the messengers herself, and they wait for her politely, because even they have heard of you.

choices.text: Ask the messengers to wait ten days

ok.log: The three confer, look at their scroll, look at the sky full of you, and sit down on the woodpile to wait. For ten days the old woman feeds them rice cakes. On the tenth the plum flowers. They all go together, and she is laughing.

fail.log: They do not bargain, even with spring. She goes that night. In the morning you flower the plum anyway, over her empty room, and her grandchildren find it and understand.

choices.text: Let them do their work. Every spring is the last for someone

effects.log: She goes. The plum flowers ten days later, as it was always going to. Her granddaughter sits under it and tells you about her. You listen. That, too, is spring.

events.text: The Black Tortoise of the north invites you, formally, through a snow goose, to spend one winter in the north with it and the snake: to see where your autumn goes when you hand it over. You have been a guardian for centuries and have never once seen winter from the inside.

choices.text: Go, and sit the whole winter on the ice

effects.log: Six months of dark and snow and the tortoise saying nothing and the snake saying everything. It is the most peaceful season of your life. When you go back south you understand spring better, the way you understand a door better from the other side.

choices.text: Decline politely. The valley needs you even in winter

effects.log: The snow goose takes your answer back north. The tortoise sends another, a hundred years later, with the same invitation, word for word. The north is patient. It will ask again.

events.text: The first full moon of a year, and you feel it the way spring feels a seed: in a village well far to the south, on the cold stones under the water, there is an egg. Blue-green, the size of a fist. At first cockcrow women will race up the lane with water jars. You were that egg, once. This one is not you. It is somebody new.

choices.text: Watch, and do nothing. That is how it was for you

effects.log: A young woman wins the race, draws the first water, floats her straw, and carries the jar home on her head, and does not know what is in it. You are spring, so you are there. You do not help. You remember being glad, later, that nobody did.

choices.text: Warm the well, so the egg does not take a chill

effects.log: The well water is warm that morning, which the women take as luck. It is. Something on the stones at the bottom stirs, very slightly, and settles, content.

events.text: The new dragonet has hatched in its water jar, lizard-sized, three claws to a foot, and has already made an enemy of the kitchen cat and a friend of the grandmother, who says do not tell. It does not know what it is. It does not know you exist. Tonight, for the first time, it lifts its head out of the jar and looks at the stars, and finds seven in the east, in a line.

choices.text: Let the seven stars shine a little brighter, once

effects.log: It looks at them all night. In the morning the grandmother finds it asleep on the rim of the jar, facing east. She says it is a good sign. She is right, though not for the reason she thinks.

choices.text: Stay as you are. It must find them itself

effects.log: The seven stars are just stars that night. It looks anyway. Some of the best things you ever did, you remember, were the ones you worked out alone.

events.text: The young dragon is in the field now, dog-sized, and has been seen: by a poor farmer who told nobody. It is frightened of the farmers' sickles and rather proud of its new horns. And it has made its first mistake: it breathed on a neighbour's field to make it green, and the drought took the rest of the valley instead, and now it lies in the paddy at night and does not understand.

choices.text: Come into its dream, once, as an old dragon would

effects.log: You say very little: that spring is not a thing you give, but a thing you share, and that every dragon learns it the hard way, and that you did too. It wakes and lies in the paddy thinking. Next year it breathes on the whole valley, thinly, and it is enough.

choices.text: Let it learn, as you learned

effects.log: It works it out by the end of summer, slowly, wrongly, then rightly. You watch it light, a hundred years later, its first star, the Horn. You are very nearly proud. You let yourself be.

choices.text: Send the White Tiger's grandchildren to keep an eye on it

effects.log: Two young white tigers turn up on the right ridge of its valley, bored and nosy. The young dragon has no idea how lucky it is. It will, in three hundred years, when they meet on a saddle between two ridges.
